audit.sourceSummary: Read the complete 736-line local primary source paper.tex, including its preamble, abstract, all 8 sections, all 15 subsections, every theorem-like environment, every proof environment, displayed mathematical examples, labels, references, and bibliography commands. Also read the complete 73-line paper.bib and confirmed that doodle.pdf is present. No article PDF is present in the supplied bundle, so exact printed page numbers could not be verified and are left null. Every explicit citation is general; none names a numbered external result, so the detailed citation-locator retrieval queue is empty and citations.statement and citations.definitions remain empty as required for general citations. The source is a LaTeX tutorial rather than a research paper, and several deliberately illustrative mathematical statements are unproved, underspecified, or false as written. Complete attached proof environments were captured directly from the local TeX tree (1 proofs), independently of the AI explanation payload.
audit.centralQuestion: How can a short sample article demonstrate the basic structure, mathematical notation, theorem environments, cross-references, citations, figures, and tables used in LaTeX?
audit.mainContribution: The paper provides a worked LaTeX source example. Its mathematical content is illustrative rather than original: it demonstrates equations and theorem/proof environments, but it does not develop a connected mathematical argument or prove its displayed theorems.
verificationWarnings: No article PDF was supplied. Exact page numbers could not be checked without generating a new file, so every page anchor is null.
Theorem 2.1 states the Pythagorean theorem but supplies no proof; the source merely inserts an end-of-proof symbol inside the theorem environment.
The displayed absolute-value definition has a dangling word “and” after the condition $x\ge 0$.

The assertion $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!\ne\prod_{j=1}^{10}j/(j+1)$ is not valid for every $x$: the right side is $1/11$, and equality holds at $x=-\log 11$. If inequality of formal expressions was intended, that convention is not stated.
The identity $[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n]^2=\exp(-x^2/2)$ does not specify the coefficients $a_n$, a convergence domain, or whether the equality is formal or analytic.
The modular-arithmetic examples use $\cong$ where congruence notation $\equiv$ is evidently intended.

Lemma 4.2 says “any graph” but the usual degree-sum formula requires a finite undirected graph and a convention that a loop contributes twice to its vertex degree. No proof or conventions are supplied.
Conjecture 4.3 is correctly presented as a conjecture, but “perfect number” is not defined in the paper and the odd-perfect-number problem is not resolved by the source.
Theorem 4.4 is false as written because it includes constant polynomials: $p(z)=1$ has complex coefficients and no zero. The standard Fundamental Theorem of Algebra requires $p$ to be nonconstant.

The freestanding proof about “interesting” integers is not a valid mathematical proof: “interesting” is undefined, and calling the least noninteresting integer interesting at the metalinguistic level does not establish the predicate used to define the set. Its placement also does not make clear whether it is merely a joke example or is meant to attach to Theorem 4.4.
Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.5 are correct under standard definitions but have no source proofs. Proposition 4.5 ends with an inserted end-of-proof symbol.
The table's definition of a singular matrix omits the usual square-matrix hypothesis; for example, a $1\times2$ matrix is not invertible but is not ordinarily classified as a singular square matrix.
No later mathematical result depends on the defective examples, so there is no downstream result-to-result warning to propagate.

nodes.label: Theorem 2.1
nodes.title: Pythagorean theorem example
nodes.statement: Suppose the lengths of the legs of a right triangle are $a$ and $b$, and the length of the hypotenuse is $c$. Then $a^2+b^2=c^2$.\qed
nodes.role: The statement is correct for a Euclidean right triangle, but the source provides no argument and instead places an end-of-proof symbol directly in the theorem environment.
proofSketch: The source states the equality and immediately inserts an end-of-proof symbol.

nodes.label: Displayed absolute-value formula
nodes.title: Piecewise formula for absolute value
nodes.statement: $$|x|=\begin{cases}x&\text{when }x\ge 0\text{ and}\\-x&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
nodes.role: The intended standard definition is clear, but the first condition ends with a dangling “and.”
nodes.whyItMatters: It demonstrates the cases environment and contains an obvious local typographical defect.

nodes.label: Displayed series-product inequality
nodes.title: Exponential-series and finite-product example
nodes.statement: $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^k}{k!}\ne\prod_{j=1}^{10}\frac{j}{j+1}.$$
nodes.role: The product telescopes to $1/11$, while the series equals $e^x$ where it converges; equality therefore occurs at $x=-\log 11$. The display needs either a qualification on $x$ or an explanation that only nonidentity of expressions is intended.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is a concrete counterexample to reading every illustrative display as a universally quantified assertion.

nodes.label: Section 3.3
nodes.title: Relations and operations
nodes.statement: Lists symbols for equality, order, arrows, sets, arithmetic, modular relations, and calculus.
nodes.role: The modular examples inconsistently use the isomorphism-like symbol $\cong$ rather than congruence $\equiv$.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is intended as a notation reference, so using the correct relation symbol is important.

nodes.label: Modular-relation display
nodes.title: Three modular-congruence formats
nodes.statement: $$\begin{aligned}x&\cong y\mod 10\\x&\cong y\pmod{10}\\x&\cong y\pod{10}\end{aligned}$$
nodes.role: The surrounding prose explicitly discusses congruence modulo $10$, making $\cong$ an inconsistent relation symbol.
nodes.whyItMatters: It distinguishes the relation symbol from the different spacing and parenthesis commands for a modulus.

nodes.label: Section 3.4
nodes.title: Use the right dots
nodes.statement: Distinguishes centered dots used between operations from baseline dots used in lists.
nodes.role: Notation and typography guidance.
nodes.whyItMatters: Correct ellipsis placement improves the semantic readability of formulas.

nodes.label: Section 3.5
nodes.title: Built up structures
nodes.statement: Demonstrates fractions, binomial coefficients, sums, products, unions, direct sums, integrals, limits, radicals, and matrices.
nodes.role: Contains the series-product inequality that fails at $x=-\log 11$.
nodes.whyItMatters: It collects the paper's main examples of vertically constructed mathematical notation.

nodes.label: Section 3.6
nodes.title: Delimiters
nodes.statement: Demonstrates parentheses, braces, norms, floor and ceiling symbols, automatically sized delimiters, manual delimiter sizes, and underbraces.
nodes.role: One display lacks hypotheses on its coefficients, and another uses a left-delimiter sizing command for a closing parenthesis.
nodes.whyItMatters: It shows both automatic and manual delimiter control while exposing two audit-sensitive examples.

nodes.label: Displayed power-series identity
nodes.title: Unspecialized Gaussian power-series identity
nodes.statement: $$\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_nx^n\right]^2=\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2}\right\}.$$
nodes.role: No values or recurrence for $a_n$ are stated, and no formal-series or analytic convergence convention is declared. It is therefore an illustrative equation rather than a justified identity.
nodes.whyItMatters: It demonstrates scalable delimiters but cannot be used as a mathematical result without additional data.

nodes.label: Manual-delimiter display
nodes.title: Comparison of delimiter-sizing commands
nodes.role: The final closing parenthesis is preceded by $\bigl$ instead of the matching right-delimiter command $\bigr$.
nodes.whyItMatters: The example is specifically intended to teach correct delimiter sizing and orientation.

nodes.label: Section 3.7
nodes.title: Styled and decorated letters
nodes.statement: Demonstrates primes, bars, hats, vectors, bold mathematical symbols, calligraphic letters, and blackboard bold.
nodes.role: Mathematical typography reference.
nodes.whyItMatters: It distinguishes semantic mathematical alphabets from text-font commands.

nodes.label: Section 3.8
nodes.title: Defining your own commands
nodes.statement: Explains reusable commands and commands with one or more arguments using number-system, column-vector, and binomial-expression examples.
nodes.role: Explains the custom-command architecture illustrated in the preamble.
nodes.whyItMatters: It encourages consistent notation and makes global notation changes possible.

nodes.label: Section 4
nodes.title: Theorem/Proof
nodes.statement: Demonstrates shared theorem numbering, named theorems, proof environments, and manually inserted end-of-proof symbols.
nodes.role: This is the paper's proof-architecture section, but most results are unproved, Theorem 4.4 is false as written, and the sole proof environment contains an invalid semantic paradox.
nodes.whyItMatters: It contains every theorem-like item central to a proof-oriented reading of the paper.

nodes.label: Theorem 4.1
nodes.title: Compact subsets of the real line
nodes.statement: A subset of the real line is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
nodes.role: This is the Heine–Borel characterization for the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$ and is mathematically correct, including for the empty set, but the source supplies no proof.
proofSketch: No proof is present in the source.
The theorem appears only as an example of shared theorem numbering.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the first result in the shared counter used by the theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, and conjecture environments.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.2
nodes.title: Degree-sum formula
nodes.statement: In any graph, the sum of the degrees of the vertices is twice the number of edges.
nodes.role: The standard double-counting proof works for finite undirected graphs when each loop contributes twice to degree. “Any graph” leaves finiteness, direction, multiple edges, and loop conventions unstated, and no proof is supplied.
proofSketch: The intended proof would count vertex-edge incidences in two ways.
Each ordinary edge contributes one incidence at each endpoint, hence two in total.
That route requires a finite incidence count and an explicit loop convention, neither of which the source states.
nodes.whyItMatters: It demonstrates shared lemma numbering but also illustrates how omitted structural hypotheses can make a familiar assertion ill-posed.

nodes.label: Proposition 4.5
nodes.title: Parity of perfect numbers
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be an integer. Then $x$ is even if and only if $x+1$ is odd.\qed
nodes.role: The source correctly labels this as a conjecture rather than a theorem, but it does not define “perfect number.” No proof is claimed or supplied.
proofSketch: No proof is given, consistently with the conjecture label.
nodes.whyItMatters: It illustrates the conjecture environment and shared numbering while remaining outside the paper's proved content.

nodes.label: Theorem 4.4
nodes.title: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then there exists $z \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $p(z)=0$.
nodes.proofText: Let $X$ be the set of all positive integers that are not interesting. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $X\not=\emptyset$. By the well-ordering principle, $X$ contains a least element $a$. Note that $a$ is the first noninteresting number, but that's interesting! $\Rightarrow\Leftarrow$. Therefore, $X=\emptyset$ and so all positive integers are interesting.
nodes.role: The conclusion is false for a nonzero constant polynomial, for example $p(z)=1$. The missing nonconstant hypothesis is substantive and is not silently repaired. No proof of the statement appears.
proofSketch: No proof route for the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra is supplied.
The nearby proof environment discusses “interesting” integers and cannot prove this theorem.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the clearest mathematical correctness failure in the source and demonstrates why theorem hypotheses must be audited independently of familiar theorem names.

nodes.label: Well-ordering principle
nodes.title: Least element of a nonempty set of positive integers
nodes.statement: The freestanding proof invokes the principle in the form: if $X$ is a nonempty set of positive integers, then $X$ contains a least element.
nodes.role: The principle is correctly applied after the proof assumes that its set $X$ is nonempty. It does not cure the undefined and self-referential predicate used to construct $X$.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the only explicit prerequisite named in the paper's sole proof environment.

nodes.label: Proof
nodes.title: Freestanding proof that all positive integers are interesting
nodes.statement: The proof claims that all positive integers are interesting by considering the least positive integer that is not interesting.
nodes.role: The proof is not attached unambiguously to a formal statement and cannot prove Theorem 4.4. As a standalone argument it is invalid because “interesting” is undefined and the metalinguistic observation that a least counterexample is interesting does not imply membership in the predicate's extension.
proofSketch: Let $X$ be the set of positive integers declared not interesting.
Assume $X\ne\varnothing$ and use well-ordering to select its least element $a$.
Call $a$ interesting because it is the first noninteresting integer.
The third step changes levels between an undefined object-language predicate and an informal metalinguistic reaction, so the contradiction is unsupported.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the paper's only complete proof environment and the main object for learning why syntactically valid proof prose need not be mathematically valid.

nodes.label: Proposition 4.5
nodes.title: Parity after adding one
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be an integer. Then $x$ is even if and only if $x+1$ is odd.
nodes.role: The assertion is correct under the standard definitions of even and odd integers, but the source supplies no derivation and inserts an end-of-proof symbol in the proposition itself.
proofSketch: A valid route would write $x=2k$ in one direction and $x+1=2k+1$ in the other, but that argument is not present in the source.
nodes.whyItMatters: It demonstrates a manually inserted end-of-proof symbol but should not be mistaken for a proved result within this document.

nodes.label: Section 5
nodes.title: Cross References
nodes.statement: Explains labels, references, page references, equation references, BibTeX keys, bibliography generation, and repeated processing.
nodes.role: All active internal labels referenced in the source are present: the section, theorem, equation, and figure references resolve at the source level.
nodes.whyItMatters: It explains the label-reference relationships preserved by this audit.

nodes.label: Section 5.1
nodes.title: Labels for numbered entities
nodes.statement: Demonstrates references to Section 5, Theorem 2.1, its page, and Equation (1).
nodes.role: Cross-reference demonstration.
nodes.whyItMatters: It identifies the two mathematical units intentionally reused elsewhere in the document.

nodes.label: Section 5.2
nodes.title: Citations
nodes.statement: Explains the role of the BibTeX file, bibliography keys, explicit citations, inclusion of uncited entries, and the processing sequence.
nodes.role: Contains one general citation to The TeXbook and no specific external locator.
nodes.whyItMatters: It explains how the bibliography records read during this audit enter the rendered document.

nodes.label: Section 6
nodes.title: Figures
nodes.statement: Explains inclusion, scaling, placement, captioning, and labeling of a PDF figure. The referenced doodle.pdf file is present in the source bundle.
nodes.role: Figure-inclusion demonstration.
nodes.whyItMatters: It verifies that the source's only external graphical dependency is available.

nodes.label: Section 7
nodes.title: Tables
nodes.statement: Provides examples of alignment, grid rules, a small value table, and a term-definition table.
nodes.role: The singular-matrix entry omits the standard square-matrix scope.
nodes.whyItMatters: It contains the paper's only explicit table of mathematical definitions.

nodes.label: Term-definition table
nodes.title: Symmetric matrix
nodes.statement: A symmetric matrix is a matrix equal to its own transpose.
nodes.role: A standard concise definition; equality with the transpose implicitly forces compatible square dimensions.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is one of the source's explicitly named mathematical definitions.

nodes.label: Term-definition table
nodes.title: Singular matrix
nodes.statement: A singular matrix is a matrix that is noninvertible.
nodes.role: The usual elementary definition applies to square matrices. Without that scope, a rectangular matrix such as a $1\times2$ matrix is noninvertible but is not ordinarily called a singular square matrix.
nodes.whyItMatters: It shows that even a short glossary definition must state the class of objects under discussion.

nodes.label: Term-definition table
nodes.title: Doubly stochastic matrix
nodes.statement: A doubly stochastic matrix is a nonnegative matrix whose rows and columns sum to one.
nodes.role: This is the standard finite-dimensional definition; the simultaneous row- and column-sum conditions force equal numbers of rows and columns.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the most structurally informative definition in the table.

nodes.label: Section 8
nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.statement: Lists general references for LaTeX, AMS mathematical packages, graphics, and TeX. It makes no citation to a specifically numbered external result.
nodes.role: Bibliographic orientation only. Each citation is general, so no external theorem statement or specialized definition is associated with it.
nodes.whyItMatters: It records every remaining explicit citation and completes the paper's source structure.

nodes.label: Conjecture 4.3
nodes.title: Conjecture
nodes.statement: All perfect numbers are even.
nodes.role: Source result preserved by the deterministic document parser.
nodes.whyItMatters: This result belongs to the complete original document structure and was retained even though the AI audit did not create a separate analytical node for it.

sourceBlocks.content: This is a simple \LaTeX\ document designed to illustrate the basics of typesetting a paper. The ideas shown here can be adapted for a more informal document, such as a homework assignment.

This document is created from various source files, the most important of which is named \verb|paper.tex|. By reading \verb|paper.tex| along side the typeset output, the diligent reader should be able to deduce how various parts of \LaTeX\ work. Indeed, you cannot understand everything that we did in this paper without looking at the source file. For example, how did we type \LaTeX?
Remember that \LaTeX\ is a markup language and not a what-you-see-is-what-you-get word processor.
Good luck.

\LaTeX\ converts files you type into professional-looking typeset documents. You type your \LaTeX\ document using a text editor (such as Emacs on a Unix computer or in an integrated editor in a \TeX\ system). This file's name should end ``\verb|.tex|''. The file that produced this document is named \verb|paper.tex|.

To convert a source file, such as \verb|paper.tex|, into a finished product (in \verb|PDF| format) one gives a command (Note: For papers with cross references it may be necessary to run `pdflatex` more than once.) such as this: \begin{verbatim} pdflatex paper \end{verbatim} An integrated \LaTeX\ system will have a menu item named ``Typeset'' (or something simimlar) to process your file.

The first line of a typical \LaTeX\ document is this: \begin{verbatim} \documentclass[12pt]{article} \end{verbatim} (The optional \verb|[12pt]| sets the overall point size for the main text of your document to 12 points. You may use \verb|[11pt]| for 11 point text or omit this for 10 point.)

The lines immediately following \verb|\documentclass| are known as the preamble of your document. This is where you define your own commands, load optional packages, etc. In the simple \verb|hello-world.tex| file, there are no lines in the preamble section. For this document, there are several.

The main text of the document is enclosed between lines that say \verb|\begin{document}| and \verb|\end{document}|. This is where you type the words you want to appear on your paper. (Look for those lines now in the file \verb|paper.tex|.)
To type ordinary text, simply type what you want. To start a new paragraph, simply skip a line.

Certain characters have special meanings. The two most important are the backslash (\verb|\|) and the dollar sign (\verb|$|). Most \LaTeX\ commands are preceded by a backslash. All mathematical symbols should be enclosed by dollar signs. If you need a dollar sign in ordinary text, you can type \verb|\$| to produce, say, ``Dan Naiman owes me \$5.'' I can't think of any occasion where you need a backslash in ordinary text. (You cannot produce a backslash in ordinary text by typing \verb|\\|.)

Use the correct quotation marks. To enclose words in double quotes, begin with two back tick characters (Note: On many keyboards, you will find the back tick character in the top row to the extreme left.) \verb|``| and end with two apostrophes \verb|''|. Do not use the double quote key \verb|"|. To enclose words in single quotes, begin with a single back tick character and end with a single apostrophe.

Typically, you should not need to change the size of the text you are typing. Use the logical structures of \LaTeX\ and let the computer pick the appropriate size. (Note: For example, text in a footnote is automatically typeset smaller than text in the main body of the document.) The overall point size of the document is indicated at the beginning of the file as an optional argument to the \verb|\documentclass| command.

Likewise with font style. In general, you do not need to pick the font. Variable names in mathematics mode are automatically typeset in italics as in $x+1$. Similiarly, the font style in section heads, theorems, etc., are automatically produced for you. For example:
Suppose the lengths of the legs of a right triangle are $a$ and $b$, and the length of the hypotenuse is $c$. Then $a^2+b^2=c^2$.\qed
However, there are times you may wish to use italics to show emphasis. To do this enclose your text in \verb|...| as in: I am still waiting for him to pay me back.
Never use mathematics mode to typeset ordinary text in italics. If you do, the result will look $awful$.

To typeset in boldface enclose your text in \verb|...| and to typeset in sans serif enclose in \verb|...|. However, you probably will not need to use these in ordinary text. (Later we talk about math typeset in bold, e.g., for vectors.)

To typeset in Caps and Small Caps use \verb|...|. To typeset in typewriter font use \verb|...|. However, to show something that looks like computer code, you probably want to use one of the verbatim methods; look inside this document to figure out how we did it. The starred version of the verbatim environment shows spaces with a \verb*|funny little symbol|.

The system of fonts used by \LaTeX\ is known as the Computer Modern family. If you prefer Times Roman, include these commands in the preamble of your file: \begin{verbatim} \usepackage{times} \usepackage{mathptm} \end{verbatim}
Don't be na\"{\i}ve, ordering \'a la carte is expensive. Don't use ö when you write Erd\H{o}s. Be honest; don't put up a façade. Use H\^opital's rule.
For numbered lists use the \verb|enumerate| enviroment and for bulleted lists use the \verb|itemize| environment as in these examples.
This is a numbered list.
• If you loan money to faculty members, be sure to get an I.O.U.
• To be sure that students show up for events, serve food.
This is a bulleted list.
• \LaTeX\ does an excellent job of typesetting mathematics papers.
• \LaTeX\ can easily produce beautiful results that are 99\% perfect.
• You can drive yourself crazy on that last 1\%. Don't bother.
You can nest these types of lists inside each other.

Whenever you typeset mathematical notation, it needs to be inside a mathematics environment. The simplest way to do this is to enclose the notation between single dollar signs \verb|$|. For example: If $a$ is an integer, then $2a+1$ is odd.
Superscripts and subscripts are created using the characters \verb|^| and \verb|_|, respectively: $x^2+y^2=1$ and $a_n=0$. It is fine to have both on a single letter: $x_0^2$.
If the superscript [or subscript] is more than a single character, enclose the superscript in curly braces: $e^{-x}$.
Greek letters are typed using commands such as \verb|\gamma| ($\gamma)$ and \verb|\Gamma| ($\Gamma$).

Named mathematics operators are usually typeset in roman. Most of the standards are already available. Some examples: $\det A$, $\cos\pi$, and $\log(1-x)$. If \LaTeX\ doesn't already have the operator you like, you can create your own (Note: This requires the amsmath package; see [[cite:amsldoc]].) using the \verb|DeclareMathOperator| command. For example, to make \verb|\operatorname{id}| the identity operator: \begin{verbatim} \DeclareMathOperator{\operatorname{id}}{id} \end{verbatim} Now we can type \verb|$\operatorname{id}(x)$| to produce $\operatorname{id}(x)$. The \verb|\DeclareMathOperator| command must go in the preamble (before \verb|\begin{document}|).

sourceBlocks.content: When an equation becomes too large to run in-line, you display it on a line by itself by enclosing it in double dollar signs \verb|$$|. $$ f(x) = 5x^{10}-9x^9 + 77x^8 + 12x^7 + 4x^6 - 8x^5 + 7x^4 + x^3 -2x^2 + 3x + 11. $$
If you want a numbered equation, enclose it in \verb| $$| and \verb|$$ |.
The numbering is automatically provided by \LaTeX.
If you want to number an equation with your own number (don't!) or symbol (maybe), you can do this: $$ h(x) = f(x)+g(x). \eqno{(*)} $$

The \verb|$$\begin{aligned}...\end{aligned}$$| environment is superb for lining up equations. (Omit the \verb|*| for numbered equations.) $$\begin{aligned} (x-y)^2 &= (x-y)(x-y)\\ &= x^2 -yx - xy + y^2 \\ &= x^2 -2xy +y^2. \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 3x-y&=0 & 2a+b &= 4 \\ x+y &=1 & a-3b &=10 \end{aligned}$$
To insert ordinary text inside of mathematics mode, use \verb|\text|: $$ f(x) = \frac{x}{x-1} \text{for }x\not=1. $$ This is the $3^{\text{rd}}$ time I've asked for my money back.
The \verb|\begin{cases}...\end{cases}| environment is perfect for defining functions piecewise: $$ |x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{when }x \ge 0\text{ and} \\ -x & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} $$
• Equality-like: $x=2$, $x \not= 3$, $x \cong y$, $x \propto y$, $y\sim z$, $N \approx M$, $y \asymp z$, $P \equiv Q$.
• Order: $x < y$, $y \le z$, $z \ge 0$, $x \preceq y$, $y\succ z$, $A \subseteq B$, $B \supset Z$.
• Arrows: $x \to y$, $y\gets x$, $A \Rightarrow B$, $A \iff B$, $x \mapsto f(x)$, $A \Longleftarrow B$.

• Set stuff: $x \in A$, $b 
otin C$, $A 
i x$. Use \verb|
otin| rather than \verb|
ot\in|. $A \cup B$, $X \cap Y$, $A \setminus B = \emptyset$.
• Arithmetic: $3+4$, $5-6$, $7\cdot 8 = 7\times8$, $3\div6=\frac{1}{2}$, $f\circ g$, $A \oplus B$, $v \otimes w$.

• Mod: As a binary operation, use \verb|\bmod|: $x \bmod N$. As a relation use \verb|\mod|, \verb|\pmod|, or \verb|\pod|: $$\begin{aligned} x &\cong y \mod 10 \\ x &\cong y \pmod{10} \\ x &\cong y \pod{10} \end{aligned}$$
• Calculus: $\partial F/\partial x$, $\nabla g$.
Do not type three periods; instead use \verb|\cdots| between operations and \verb|\ldots| in lists: $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n$ and $(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$.
• Fractions: $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{x-1}{x-2}$.
• Binomial coefficients: $\binom{n}{2}$.

• Sums and products. Do not use \verb|\Sigma| and \verb|\Pi|. $$ \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{x^k}{k!} \not= \prod_{j=1}^{10} \frac{j}{j+1}. $$ $$ \bigcup_{k=0}^\infty A_k \qquad \bigoplus_{j=1}^\infty V_j $$
• Integrals: $$ \int_0^1 x^2 \, dx $$ The extra bit of space before the $dx$ term is created with the \verb|\,| command.
• Limits: $$ \lim_{h\to0} \frac{\sin(x+h) - \sin(x)}{h} = \cos x . $$ Also $\limsup_{n\to\infty} a_n$.
• Radicals: $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt[3]{12}$, $\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}$.

• Matrices: $$ A = \left[\begin{matrix} 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & \pi \end{matrix}\right] . $$ In line: $A = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. A big matrix: $$ D = \left[ \begin{matrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \lambda_3 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_n \end{matrix} \right]. $$
• Parentheses and square brackets are easy: $(x-y)(x+y)$, $[3-x]$.
• For curly braces use \verb|\{| and \verb|\}|: $\{x : 3x-1 \in A\}$.
• Absolute value: $|x-y|$, $\|\vec{x} - \vec{y}\|$.
• Floor and ceiling: $\lfloor \pi \rfloor = \lceil e \rceil$.

• To make delimiters grow so they are properly sized to contain their arguments, use \verb|\left| and \verb|\right|: $$ \left[ \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n \right]^2 = \exp \left\{ - \frac{x^2}{2} \right\} $$

Occasionally, it is useful to coerce a larger sized delimiters than \verb|\left|/\verb|\right| produce. Look at the two sides of this equation: $$ \left((x_1+1)(x_2-1)\right) = \bigl((x_1+1)(x_2-1)\bigl). $$ I think the right is better. Use \verb|\bigl|, \verb|\Bigl|, \verb|\biggl|, and the matching \verb|\bigr|, etc.
• Underbraces: $$ \underbrace{1+1+\cdots+1}_{n\text{ times}} = n . $$
• Primes: $a'$, $b''$.
• Hats: $\bar a$, $\hat a$, $\vec a$, $\widehat{a_j}$.
• Vectors are often set in bold: $\mathbf{x}$. Don't use \verb|\textbf| in mathematics mode and don't use \verb|\mathbf| in text mode.
• Calligraphic letters (for sets of sets): $\mathcal{A}$.
• Blackboard bold for number systems: $\mathbb{C}$.

You can (and should) define your own commands (also called macros). For example, if you refer to the positive orthant $\mathbb{R}^n_+$ frequently, put the following line in your preamble: \begin{verbatim} \newcommand{\mathbb{R}^n_+}{\mathbb{R}^n_+} \end{verbatim} Then, you can just type \verb|$\mathbb{R}^n_+$| instead of \verb|$\mathbb{R}^n_+$|. Also, if later you decide that you prefer $\mathbf{R}$ instead of $\mathbb{R}$, you only have to change the definition of \verb|\mathbb{R}^n_+|.

It is possible to define commands that take arguments. For example, suppose your paper uses column vectors frequently. We define a new command named \verb|\left[\begin{matrix} | \end{matrix} \right] like this: \begin{verbatim} \newcommand{\left[\begin{matrix} } \end{matrix} \right][1]{\left[\begin{matrix} #1 \end{matrix} \right]} \end{verbatim} The \verb|[1]| means that \verb|\left[\begin{matrix} | \end{matrix} \right] takes one argument. The \verb|#1| shows where that one argument goes. Now we can type $$ \left[\begin{matrix} 1\\2\\3 \end{matrix} \right] + \left[\begin{matrix} -1\\3\\-2 \end{matrix} \right] = \left[\begin{matrix} 0\\5\\1 \end{matrix} \right] $$ easily.

Here's another example. Suppose the expression $\binom{a^2 + b^2}{a+b}$ appears often (but with different values for $a$ and $b$). Let's call the combinatorial oddity \verb|\binom{|^2 + a^2}{|+a}nd define it like this: \begin{verbatim} \newcommand{\binom{}^2 + [^2}{}+[}2]{\binom{#1^2 + #2^2}{#1+#2}} \end{verbatim} and use it like this: \verb|$\binom{a^2 + b^2}{a+b}$|.

The first line defines a \verb|\begin{thm}...\end{thm}| environment. This will produce a theorem named ``Theorem'' and the numbering style will be based on the section (e.g., Theorem 2.1); omit the \verb|[section]| and the numbering will be absolute (e.g., Theorem 1).
The second line defines a \verb|\begin{lem}...\end{lem}| environment to produce theorems marked ``Lemma''. The \verb|[thm]| means that this environment shares the same numbering as \verb|thm|.
So we get this:
A subset of the real line is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
In any graph, the sum of the degrees of the vertices is twice the number of edges.
All perfect numbers are even.

Let $x$ be an integer. Then $x$ is even if and only if $x+1$ is odd.\qed

Numbered \LaTeX\ structures can be given a label and we can use that label to refer to that structure. For example, this section is labeled using the command \verb||. That enables me to type \verb|Section the referenced result| to produce ``Section the referenced result''. The tilde \verb| | is called a ``tie'' character. It produces a space but \LaTeX\ won't break the line at that point.

It is much better to use labels and references than to type in the section (or theorem or subsection or figure or equation) number yourself. If you change the document, the labels will change automatically.
You can use \verb|\pageref| to give the page number on which the label can be found. For example, Theorem the referenced result is on page \pageref{thm:pyth}. Don't use this for journal submissions.
You can use \verb|\eqref| to refer to equations; this command inserts the parentheses for you: The polynomial $g$ is defined in Equation the referenced result.
Most papers contain references. The best way to deal with references in \LaTeX\ is as follows:

• Have a separate bibtex file; the bibtex file for this paper is named \verb|paper.bib|. The bibtex file contains all the information about the references but no formatting information. Examine the \verb|paper.bib| file that accompanies this document.
• At the end of the paper, please find these lines \begin{verbatim}
\end{verbatim} The first specifies the bibliography style. (We chose ``plain'' but there are others available.) The second builds the actual References section of the paper.

• Each entry in the bibtex file has a key name. For example, the key for Knuth's \TeX book is \verb|knuth84|. To include a reference in the paper to this book, we type \verb|[[cite:knuth84]]| to give this: [[cite:knuth84]].

• Normally, only references that are cited with a \verb|\cite| command appear in the paper's bibliography. However, to coerce \LaTeX\ to include all references in the bibtex file into your bibliography, include the command \verb|| just after the \verb|\begin{document}| command.
To process the files \verb|paper.tex| and \verb|paper.bib|, run these commands on your computer: \begin{verbatim} pdflatex paper bibtex paper pdflatex paper pdflatex paper \end{verbatim}

To incorporate a diagram into \LaTeX\ you first prepare that diagram in a separate drawing program such as \verb|xfig|, Mathematica, or Matlab. Save your illustration in \verb|pdf| format; let's say the file is called \verb|doodle.pdf|. We now want it to appear in our paper (as Figure the referenced result).

sourceBlocks.content: The \LaTeX\ code that make the figure appear is this: \begin{verbatim}
[Figure from the original source: doodle]
A doodle created with the Xfig program.
\end{verbatim}

The optional \verb|[ht]| means that the figure may appear either ``Here'' or else at the ``Top'' of the next page (if it doesn't fit here). \LaTeX\ takes these as suggestions and may decide to put your figure somewhere else if the figure is too big.

The optional \verb|[scale=0.5]| shrinks the image by 50\%. Try \verb|[width=\textwidth]| to make the figure exactly as wide as your text. Or \verb|[width=0.75\textwidth]| makes it $\frac34$ of the width of your text.
